A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same neural approach to Hadwiger-Nelson coloring problems. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–F are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original neural-network experiments, numerical conflict rates, and discovered colorings for planar, off-diagonal, three-dimensional, triangle-avoidance, and alternative-norm problems.

after.justification: v2 retains original numerical experiments and adds periodic almost-coloring evaluations and results from its automated formalization procedure.

M1.justification: v2 introduces Algorithm 1: extract periodicity, retrain with an exact periodic coordinate mapping, discretize the output, and repair conflicts through recoloring. It also applies this procedure in three dimensions. This substantially extends the procedure beyond v1's neural optimization and subsequent human formalization; the original losses remain.

E1.justification: v2 explicitly evaluates the almost-coloring objective in three dimensions, whereas v1 reports ordinary 14-color candidates and only proposes converting them into almost-colorings. Table 1 also extends planar almost-coloring coverage to one color. The existing four variants and alternative-norm examples remain.

E2.justification: Section 5 newly reports experiments with Fourier bases and Voronoi diagrams, stating that neural networks performed best. These are additional evaluated alternatives, although the comparison is qualitative and supplies no scores or matched experimental settings.

E3.justification: Table 1 replaces evaluation in a finite [-3,3]^2 box with evaluation on a parallelogram under periodic boundary conditions and adds formal verification through Algorithm 1. Reported hidden-layer widths change from 64–256 to 32–256, and the useful penalty range expands from 10^-3–10^-2 to 10^-3–10^-1. These are reported setting changes, without establishing that all retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: A new Section 3 footnote reports limited tests of Gaussian spatial sampling instead of uniform box sampling, finding no improved constructions. Section 5 adds qualitative sensitivity observations concerning architecture, penalty scale, and box size. The triangle conflict-threshold analysis in Appendix E was already present.

E5.justification: v1's Table 1 explicitly reports the best of 60 runs; v2 removes that run-count and selection disclosure. The general experimental description changes from hundreds to thousands of runs to thousands of runs, without establishing a specific increase. Neither version supplies confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces numerical entries and adds formalized results: the five-color entry changes from 4.01% in a finite box to 3.60% numerically under periodic evaluation and 3.74% formalized, specified as 3.7356% in the text. These are not same-setting performance comparisons. Section 4.3 newly reports 2.3% numerical conflicts and a formal almost-14-coloring excluding 3.4622% of space. The formal triangle-bound regions also change between v1 Figure 3 and v2 Figure 4. Some prior-bound entries change beyond rounding, including 0.0143% to 0.02% for six colors.

T1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Appendix B add a mathematical construction using periodic parallelogram cells and explain reducing continuous unit-distance avoidance to stricter discrete cell constraints. Proposition 3.1, its proof, and the existing loss formulations remain unchanged. No separate new theorem or complete construction proof is supplied.

C1.justification: The introduction adds formal almost-colorings in two and three dimensions to the principal contributions, including the improved five-color bound. It also expands the claimed discovery process to include fully automated formalization in selected cases. v1 left these almost-coloring constructions tentative; the central off-diagonal six-coloring claim is retained.

C2.justification: v2 explains how freedom to enlarge the removed region enables automated formalization, discusses neural representations' advantages and tuning limitations, and identifies finer discretization as a possible improvement for the three-dimensional construction. It also qualifies the 15-color numerical solutions as near conflict-free. The existing interpretations concerning chromatic and polychromatic numbers remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a repository link for reproduction code and formalized constructions. Appendix B supplies previously absent instructions for detecting periodicity through translated radial evaluations, constructing cell conflict masks, and repairing conflicts. Reported runtimes are also revised, including V100 runs from 5–20 to 2–20 minutes, without a controlled timing comparison.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to AlphaEvolve, Alfarano et al., Trinh et al., Gwyn and Stavrianos, and Croft, extending the discovery-method context and attribution of prior coloring bounds. The main positioning relative to combinatorial optimization and implicit neural representations remains. Several other reference changes merely update publication metadata.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution list are reorganized, the discussion is expanded, an Impact Statement is added, and terminology and prose receive local corrections. The section sequence, four-variant organization, and substantial portions of the narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figure 2 and an Algorithm 1 display, expands Table 1, and replaces Appendix B's numerical coloring displays with six formalized periodic constructions. It redraws the formal triangle-bound diagram, recolors other triangle plots, enlarges the three-dimensional visualization, and moves v1 Figure 7 into Appendix C as Figure 13. Together these substantially revise the presentation of constructions and verification.

improvement.justification: v1 left the five-color and three-dimensional almost-colorings unformalized. v2 substantially addresses that gap through Algorithm 1, Appendix B's procedural explanation, separately reported numerical and formalized results, and code-access information. This strengthens the connection between neural exploration and checkable mathematical constructions. Full construction accounts remain deferred and Table 1 loses explicit run-count detail, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in methodological completeness and evidential clarity.
